stories.title: A burial row over Zambia's late president has turned its election into a hot contest
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, More than eight million registered voters have 14 presidential candidates to choose from By Dingindaba Buyoya BBC Focus on Africa ,Â Reporting from Lusaka Published 2 hours ago A spectre is hanging over the Zambian election campaign in the shape of former President Edgar Lungu. Despite having died more than a year ago in South Africa, his body remains unburied amid a bitter dispute between President Hakainde Hichilema and the Lungu family that has sharpened political divisions. This has had a role in energising support for the opposition National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), particularly in the northern half of the country, traditional strongholds of Lungu's Patriotic Front (PF), as people see it as offering the best chance to unseat the incumbent. Meanwhile, it has complicated the second-term bid of Hichilema and his United Party for National Development (UPND), which draws its core support from the south, west and north-west while seeking to expand its reach nationwide. The political battle is playing out on the streets of the capital, Lusaka.

stories.title: Somalia: UN Puts Somalia Mission Assets Up for Sale As U.S. Funding Cutoff Looms
stories.summary: Somalia: UN Puts Somalia Mission Assets Up for Sale As U.S. Funding Cutoff Looms Pixabay United Nations, UN Flag 10 August 2026 Radio Dalsan (Mogadishu) By Abdirazak Gesey Mogadishu, Somalia — The United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has opened a tender seeking licensed auctioneers to sell off a wide range of its vehicles, generators and other equipment in Somalia, a notice published on the UN Global Marketplace shows. The call for expressions of interest, issued August 6, comes as Washington moves to cut off funding for the UN's logistical support mission by the end of 2026, deepening uncertainty over the future of international backing for Somalia's fight against al-Shabab. The tender matters now because it lands at the center of a widening rift between the United States and the United Nations over how and whether, to keep supporting Somalia's security transition. UNSOS underpins the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), supplying transport, fuel, food and other non-lethal supplies to roughly 12,000 African troops and police fighting a resilient insurgency.

stories.title: Malawi: Bombshell Land Audit to Name Ministers, Judges and MPs Over Illegal Plot Grabs
stories.summary: Malawi: Bombshell Land Audit to Name Ministers, Judges and MPs Over Illegal Plot Grabs 10 August 2026 Nyasa Times (Leeds) Malawi's Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development is set to hold a highly anticipated press briefing this Wednesday to unveil the findings of a pilot land ownership audit conducted in Lilongwe - findings that are set to implicate some of the country's most powerful figures. According to an invitation letter seen by this publication, Minister of Lands Chimwemwe Chipungu will personally preside over the briefing, which is expected to shed light on widespread irregularities uncovered during the audit process. 'The Ministry embarked on the Land Ownership Audit exercise in February 2026 as part of efforts to strengthen land administration systems, promote accountability in land ownership and enhance transparency and efficiency in the management of land resources,' the invitation reads. The audit is understood to have uncovered significant irregularities in the allocation of plots specifically within Lilongwe's Area 3 and Area 10, two of the capital's most sought-after and valuable residential districts. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Most explosively, the audit has reportedly named a string of politically exposed individuals - including ministers serving in both the current and former administrations, sitting judges, and members of parliament - among those alleged to have acquired plots in the affected areas without following proper procedure. The revelations, if confirmed at Wednesday's briefing, threaten to ignite a fresh political storm in Malawi, given the seniority of those reportedly implicated and the sensitivity surrounding land allocation in a country where access to prime urban plots has long been a source of controversy and allegations of favouritism.

stories.summary: Uganda: Govt Orders Bus Drivers to Switch After Long Journeys to Curb Fatigue Kampala Capital City Authority/X A warden controlling traffic in Kampala. 10 August 2026 Nile Post (Kampala) By Victor Tayebwa and Jacobs Seaman Odongo The government has introduced new measures requiring bus operators to change drivers after long-distance journeys, as authorities intensify efforts to curb driver fatigue following a series of fatal road crashes in recent weeks. stories.summary: Uganda's Widows Need More Than Laws On Matters Land 10 August 2026 The Independent (Kampala) By Sheila Catherine Abamu Is the Legal Manager, Kcb Bank Uganda Ltd. The gap we face today is no longer primarily legislative; it is a crisis of enforcement, awareness, and institutional practice A familiar, heartbreaking scene plays out across Ugandan courts, local council offices, and family compounds every single week. Within days of his burial, his widow who has farmed the family land, raised children there, and contributed to the household for decades watches as her in-laws arrive to take over the property. The WHO African Region accounts for about 95% of global malaria cases and deaths. More than half of all malaria deaths in the region occur in Nigeria (31.9%), the Democratic Republic of Congo (11.7%) and Niger (6.1%). Children under 5 years of age account for about 76% of malaria deaths in the region. To stem the tide of malaria cases across Africa, the global health body has recommended a wider use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine among children living in regions with moderate to high malaria transmission by the Plasmodium falciparum — a parasite that causes 95% of all malaria infections in Africa .

The whistleblower, a prominent local fuel importer speaking on condition of anonymity, warned that his own ordeal represents merely the tip of the iceberg, cautioning that Malawi risks being flooded by unscrupulous local and international operators unless authorities dramatically tighten regulatory enforcement. He called on every relevant stakeholder - including the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority (MERA), National Oil Company of Malawi (NOCMA), Petroleum Importers Limited (PIL), Malawi Revenue Authority (MRA) and Malawi Bureau of Standards (MBS) - to urgently coordinate their efforts and clamp down on the growing threat. 'Otherwise we risk having chaos in the fuel sector in Malawi,' the whistleblower warned, visibly alarmed at the speed with which the problem appears to be escalating. He went on to expose the scale of the deception already taking place within the industry. 'There is a presence of so many unscrupulous players, especially international importers seeking to exploit many gaps in the sector,' he said. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters ‘We have no tents or blankets’: Ceuta migrants struggle to survive brutal heat and freezing nights Authorities wrestle with fallout from mass border crossing, as tense Spanish enclave fears it will happen again Along the wide avenues and tree-lined plazas of Ceuta’s centre, there were few hints of the recent events that catapulted the Spanish enclave on the north African coast into global headlines. But less than a mile away from the bustling bars and restaurants, at the nearby El Trampolín beach, the lingering impact was impossible to ignore. “We’re sleeping here on the beach, out in the open, without tents or blankets,” said Imad, 26, one of several thousand people believed to be still in Ceuta after last week’s extraordinary influx of more than 72,000 migrants into the Spanish territory on the edge of Morocco . “We don’t have bathrooms,” added the Yemen national. “I barely manage two hours of sleep, as it’s incredibly cold by the sea at night, and during the day the heat is unbearable.” View image in fullscreen A man prays inside a makeshift mosque marked out with stones on El Trampolín beach in Ceuta, where hundreds of migrants have been sheltering. Photograph: Okba Mohammad One week on, while questions continue to swirl over what exactly prompted the incident, the city’s shops and markets have reopened and many of the 84,000 residents have resumed their daily routines.

"This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC. Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan. She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023. El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October. For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare â with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food.

stories.title: What's behind the Algeria-Morocco rivalry?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5IMUo Some 60,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco several days ago Image: Ian Whittaker/News Licensing/IMAGO Advertisement Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez traveled to Algeria on July 20 for talks with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb. The meeting's aim was to resolve a diplomatic row that erupted between both countries in 2022 after Spain sided with Morocco's autonomy proposal to resolve the Western Sahara conflict — much to Algeria's dismay. It is a matter of debate whether Spain's rapprochement with Algeria outraged Morocco so much that it deliberately allowed tens of thousands of migrants to storm the Spanish exclave of Ceuta , even though both countries have improved their relations enormously in recent years. Spanish daily El Pais has certainly entertained the possibility of Moroccan meddling. "Ceuta tensions coincided with Pedro Sanchez's trip to Algeria, a regional rival of the [Moroccan] Alawite Kingdom," an opinion piece in the Spanish paper notes. The article later states that "any attempt to use immigration as a bargaining chip is unacceptable." Moroccan interior ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi has rejected such accusations, saying the incident resulted from "the malicious exploitation of the digital space," as well as "misleading information" and misinterpretations of a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling on the rights of arriving migrants.

stories.title: Spain’s Pedro Sánchez is a progressive outlier in Europe – and over Ceuta, he is being made to pay for it | Eoghan Gilmartin
stories.summary: Pedro Sánchez speaking in Ceuta, Spain, last week. ‘He called out the ‘prejudice, misinformation and attacks’ of many of his [EU] peers.’ Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters View image in fullscreen Pedro Sánchez speaking in Ceuta, Spain, last week. ‘He called out the ‘prejudice, misinformation and attacks’ of many of his [EU] peers.’ Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/Reuters Spain’s Pedro Sánchez is a progressive outlier in Europe – and over Ceuta, he is being made to pay for it Eoghan Gilmartin The Spanish PM has been one of few European leaders to stand up to Trump. He now faces coercive diplomacy and an emboldened far right at home T he dramatic footage last Thursday of thousands of migrants entering Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta generated an online frenzy among the far right. And the alarmist rhetoric was also evident in the European mainstream, as EU leaders wasted little time attributing the chaotic scenes to Spain’s liberal immigration policies. In a letter organised by Italy and Denmark, and signed by 22 EU heads of government, they appeared to blame the crisis on Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s recent programme to regularise undocumented migrants, which received more than a million applications . They argued that Europe must “[address] all policies that can serve as pull factors”.

stories.title: Fact check: Did misleading claims about Spain's migration law trigger the Ceuta crisis?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5IG1B Tens of thousands of people attempted to cross from Morocco into Ceuta during a major migration surge that authorities linked, among other factors, to misleading information circulating online Image: Antonio Sempere/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Misleading social media posts appear to have contributed to a sudden surge in migrant crossings into Spain's North African exclave of Ceuta . Tens of thousands of people attempted to cross from Morocco in late July . According to authorities, dozens drowned or were killed in crowd-related incidents during the crossings, which triggered a major humanitarian crisis. European, Spanish and Moroccan authorities blamed the sudden surge in crossings on incorrect information circulating on social media and human traffickers. A recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling on migrant returns became the focus of many of the misleading claims.

Photograph: Aaron Ufumeli/EPA El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next year UN forecasters warn of worsening conditions in 45 countries currently experiencing severe food insecurity About 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by the rapidly developing El Niño weather system , according to forecasting. This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts of Africa and pressure on food prices from the war in Iran. Even if the forecast El Niño is less strong than some models predict, it will tip many countries over the edge, adding more than a fifth to the 225 million people in 45 countries currently in acute food insecurity, the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Wednesday.

Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones People hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100 H undreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down. Their perch was the same small tranche of land that made headlines around the world last week as extraordinary scenes emerged of about 72,000 people making their way into Ceuta , a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa. stories.title: Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images By Thomas Mukhwana Africa correspondent ,Â Reporting from Amboseli Published 5 August 2026 News that the recent deaths of 15 elephants may have been caused by pesticides sprayed on tomato crops surrounding Amboseli National Park has raised concerns and questions in Kenya. Last week, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said that some of the elephants that had died between 24 June and 24 July had shown signs of "partial paralysis" that pointed to poisoning from cyanide used in pesticides. But conservationists have told the BBC that, perhaps, is not the full story. Farmers we have spoken to in the area were also sceptical. "We have stayed with this wildlife for decades and have never experienced this," Daniel Nina, who represents some of the landowners in the area, told the BBC. "So that's why we are wondering why it is happening today." The tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in the south of Kenya. It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water.
